summary: An experimental document that describes IPP from a high level, provides a roadmap to the suite of IPP specifications, and gives background and rationale for the working group's major decisions.

eli5.summary: This explains why the printing-over-the-internet rules were designed the way they were, and which documents to read in which order.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what is the ipp job id
subtitle: The reasoning behind how the Internet Printing Protocol splits into a model, an encoding and an HTTP transport.

tldr.problem: Printing over the Internet needed a protocol, and the working group had to explain why it was built from a separate model, a binary encoding and an HTTP transport, and how the set of IPP documents fits together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a high-level view of IPP, a roadmap to the suite of IPP documents, and the reasons for each major design choice: an abstract model, a simple binary encoding, HTTP 1.1 POST as transport, a directory schema, and digest authentication plus SSL3 for security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The IESG note says a revised version was expected to be published as a Proposed Standard, with stronger authentication and privacy features and an ipp: URL type, and that implementors were warned the future protocol might not interoperate.

today: RFC 2568 is an Experimental RFC from April 1999 and is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It explains the design of IPP/1.0 and points to RFC 2565 and RFC 2566 for the specifications themselves.

sections.title: The IPP Document Suite
sections.content:
RFC 2568 is one of a set of documents that together describe the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), an application level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies. This one gives the high-level view, a roadmap to the rest of the suite and the rationale for the IETF working group's major decisions.

The suite is: Design Goals (RFC 2567), this rationale document, Model and Semantics (RFC 2566), Encoding and Transport (RFC 2565), an Implementer's Guide, and a mapping between LPD and IPP (RFC 2569). Operator and administrator requirements are out of scope for IPP version 1.0.
sections.eli5: Think of a big instruction booklet split into chapters. This chapter is the one that says which chapter to read next and why the booklet was written this way.

sections.title: Architecture and the Printer
sections.content:
IPP defines interactions between a client and a server. A client can ask about a printer's capabilities, submit print jobs, and ask about or cancel jobs. The server is the Printer, an abstraction of a generic document output device and/or a print service provider. It could be a real device such as a computer printer or fax output device, or a service in front of such devices. The design is heavily influenced by the printing model of the Document Printing Application (DPA) standard, and IPP/1.0 focuses only on end user functionality.

The architecture has three layers of definition: an abstract Model of the data that controls printing, an encoding that flattens and sequences that hierarchical data, and a protocol that carries the encoded requests and responses. A typical exchange is a create-job request: the client assembles Model data such as the job name, the media and pages per sheet, encodes it, and sends it. The Printer decodes it and either accepts or rejects the job, then answers in the same way.

The model document also defines a Directory Schema, a standard set of Printer attributes (a subset of the Model attributes) that can be associated with a Printer's URI, so a client can query a directory service for a suitable Printer. For the Printer itself, the RFC assumes a minimal implementation: an output device with a specialized real time operating system and limited processing, memory and storage, connected with at least TCP/IP and likely SNMP support, and likely acting as an HTML/HTTP server.
sections.eli5: You tell the printer what you want in a form, the printer says yes or no, and there is a phone book where you can look up printers. The printer might be a small machine with not much brainpower.

sections.title: Why a Separate Abstract Model
sections.content:
The Model is defined independently of any encoding. Products can keep the Model data in an internal data structure and use a parser or formatter to convert to and from the encoded form, so the application does not depend on the encoding. That independence would let a different encoding or transport be adopted later if the chosen ones proved limiting, and lets a server accept jobs through, for example, a direct client-less GUI.

An abstract Model also lets the data line up with the model used in the Printer, Job and Host Resources MIBs, so the data is interpreted consistently whether obtained through IPP or through SNMP.

One aspect gets extra explanation: a Job can be identified either by a Job URI or by the Printer URI plus a Job ID, a 32 bit positive integer. A Job URI allows flexibility, for example moving a job from a busy printer to a lighter one without changing its identifier. But many existing systems can only use a 32-bit integer, unique only within the Printer that received the create request. So the Printer generates both for every new Job, which lets all clients work regardless of local constraints.
sections.eli5: The rules about what a print job is are written separately from how the message travels, like a recipe that works whether you send it by letter or phone. Each job gets two names so both old and new programs can find it.

sections.title: Why a Simple Binary Encoding
sections.content:
To make embedded printers simpler to build, the protocol uses a very simple binary encoding. It is a sequence of attributes. Each attribute has a name prefixed by a name length, and a value. Names are strings limited to a subset of ASCII. Values are scalars or sequences of scalars, and each scalar has a length and a value tag giving its type, split into a major class such as integer or string and a minor class such as a dateTime string. The tags allow new value types to be introduced later.

A complete request or response carries a version number, an operation (request) or a status and optional status message (response), parameters and attributes holding the encoded Model data, and optionally, for a request, print data after the Model data.
sections.eli5: The message is a simple list of labelled boxes: each box says its name, how long it is, and what kind of thing is inside. That is easy for even a small printer to read.

sections.title: Why HTTP 1.1 POST
sections.content:
The encoded Model data travels in an HTTP 1.1 POST and its response, with no changes to HTTP 1.1 proposed or required. The RFC says the most important reason is that HTTP is already widely deployed, so many problems of working across local nets, intranets and the Internet have been solved. It adds that most of the reasons could be met by other mechanisms and makes no claim that the list uniquely determines the choice.

  • Persistent connections make a multi-message protocol efficient, for example separate Create-Job and Send-Document messages.
  • Chunking lets large print files be sent without knowing the length in advance.
  • Accept headers carry the client's protocol and localization wishes, and HTTP redirects can tell a client a job has moved.
  • Network printers typically run an HTTP server anyway to serve HTML help and status.
  • Most of HTTP 1.1's complexity is in proxies, not in clients and servers.
  • URL handling, the extension model (headers, media types, error codes) and prototyping tools such as CGI scripts come for free.

POST was chosen because its use for sending data is established. A new method would have identified the use better but been harder to deploy, so a new default port gives the identification with minimal impact on installed infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new way to send mail, the designers used the web's delivery system, which already works almost everywhere and which most printers already speak.

sections.title: Security Rationale
sections.content:
The RFC notes that security is an area of active work and that complete solutions to a wide range of concerns were not yet available. The design therefore sticks to security features that are implemented or currently implementable and that solve real problems with distributed printing: authorization to use a Printer, and secure interaction with a Printer.

The chosen mechanisms are HTTP 1.1 digest authentication and SSL3 secure communication. The RFC itself notes that SSL3 is not on the IETF standards track. The IESG note expects a standards-track version to add strong authentication and privacy features, and encourages experimentation with Transport Layer Security (RFC 2246) as a security layer for IPP.
sections.eli5: To stop strangers from printing on your printer or reading your pages, the designers used locks that already existed for the web instead of making new ones.
